David Pincus  

This is a fascinating book. Walter Freeman has taken the most vexing problem in neuroscience today and has offered a compelling and well-reasoned explanation. How does a mind emerge from a brain? Schopenhauer called a version of this problem the universal knot, and there are thousands of years of discussion about how the mental relates to the physical, the age-old mind–body problem. Freeman's answer is based upon empirical research, and this makes this book far more compelling than mere conjecture. The author travels from the dynamics of olfaction in rabbits and cats to the neurodynamically generated global states we associate with emotion and consciousness, to create a coherent and scalable model of not only how brains work, but how brain functions become minds. But beware: modularism, naïve determinisms, and psychological or material reductionisms-essentialisms die a painful death in this book, and are replaced with neurodynamics, chaotic attractors, and the emergent-global properties that we think of as mentality. However, the psychoanalytic reader should not be concerned that psychic determinism is completely lost: While Freeman's model of the brain-mind supports the position of an endless contextualism that is often identified with postmodern sensibilities, there remains plenty of room for the engine house of an unconscious and the very necessary notions of transference, repetition compulsions, and defenses. It is just that all of our categories and tendencies are endlessly drenched in contextual updating, and those most pathological tend to resist this process the most. But this viewpoint should be familiar and congruent with most principles of psychopathology and psychoanalytic thought.

Freeman has devoted his life to neurobiological research, and is an emeritus professor in the graduate school at the University of California, Berkeley. He has been a valued teacher and done research at Berkeley for more than 40 years. In this book, which builds upon more than 350 research articles and papers and his two previous books Mass Action in the Nervous System and Societies of Brains (1995), Freeman moves effortlessly between the fields of neurobiology, philosophy, the history of science, engineering, computer science, and nonlinear dynamics to weave together a comprehensive explanation to the universal knot. Part of Freeman's task is to appeal to a wide audience and not merely to those interested in a particular discipline, and to balance breadth with the appropriate level of depth. Interdisciplinary studies are tricky that way, as depth in one area can become alienating to one reader, but too much breadth can seem to only cover the surface.

Susan Loden  

The Second International Neuro-Psychoanalysis Congress, held at the New York Academy of Medicine, focused on memory from the perspectives of cognitive neuroscience research and psychoanalysis. This congress, like last year's on emotion, attracted a large number of delegates from around the world with both the psychoanalytic and neuroscientific communities well represented. The topic of memory is clearly of central concern to both disciplines, and debate at the congress highlighted not only areas of convergence, along with areas of disagreement, which could lead to potentially fruitful further research, but also the complexity of the subject and some problems in establishing basic working definitions and rules of evidence acceptable to both neuroscientists and psychoanalysts.

The congress was opened by Karl Pribram, distinguished neuroscientist, a founder of the discipline of neuropsychology, and author of Languages of the Brain and Brain and Perception: Holonomy and Structure in Figural Processing. Professor Pribram gave a brief overview of his work on the neural concomitants of consciousness, developments based on quantum holography. He stressed that Freud started from a biologically based model founded on neuroscience—in his view the “Project” is the Rosetta stone for the whole language of psychoanalysis—but signaled that his own work has taken quite a different direction. For example, Freud emphasized selective memory; in Pribram's view the concept of repression (as something pushed down and hidden) is not viable.

The problem of “the repressed,” the acceptance or not of the concept of a dynamic unconscious, was a leitmotif of the congress, the core of a controversy separating the two disciplines. There seemed at times to be some difficulty in finding a common language. The two main papers given by cognitive scientists took as their subject memory distortion and false memory. Daniel Schacter, Chair and Professor of Psychology, Harvard University, who coined the term implicit memory, spoke on “the seven sins of memory” in terms of false memories, misattributions, and false recognitions. He demonstrated how easy it is to implant a false memory for a word in a significant proportion of the audience (including this member of it), but he added that misattributions are based on a healthy memory system which is adaptive. Memory distortion does not indicate a fundamental flaw: Errors of categorization and generalization are necessary for the mind to function at an abstract level. Professor Schacter did not draw conclusions for psychoanalysis from his research but reinforced the notion that memory is nonveridical, and that the implicit memory system recategorizes the present in terms of the past.
